task_classes.name: Session Storage Backend
task_classes.description: Build the Postgres/AGE session storage layer that replaces Claude Code's file-based JSONL system. Learn SDK foundations (query, tools, messages, options) by building the ingestion pipeline and backend abstraction.

tasks.description: Worked Example: Anatomy of a Claude Code session. Read the SDK session internals (_internal/sessions.py), understand JSONL format, parentUuid DAG structure. Walk through query() → message iteration → ResultMessage extraction. Build mental model of the complete data flow.

Worked Example: Build the session ingestion tool. Create @tool functions for Postgres + AGE operations. Wire into create_sdk_mcp_server. Use query() to drive an agent that reads a JSONL file and ingests it into Postgres, preserving the parentUuid tree as AGE graph edges.

Guided: Build the backend abstraction layer. Design the interface that lets BHappy toggle between file-based and DB-backed session storage. Implement the DB reader (list_sessions, get_session_messages equivalent from Postgres). Test both backends produce identical results.

Conventional: Fork and rewind from DB. Implement fork-at-arbitrary-turn by creating a new branch in the AGE parentUuid tree. Implement rewind by querying the tree up to a specific message UUID. Test with real BHappy worker session transcripts.

Mastery Gate: End-to-end demo. Ingest 5 real BHappy worker sessions, query them from Postgres, fork one at turn 3, rewind another to a specific tool use. Demonstrate file↔DB toggle with identical output. Explain the AGE graph model and query patterns used.

mastery_gate.criteria: Can ingest JSONL sessions into Postgres/AGE, query them back, fork/rewind at arbitrary points, and toggle between file and DB backends. Can explain parentUuid DAG structure and AGE graph model.

task_classes.name: Cost & Observability Instrumentation
task_classes.description: Add cost tracking, structured tool-use logging, and distributed tracing to BHappy. Fix the permissions misconception. Build the observability layer that's currently missing.

tasks.description: Productive Failure: Permissions architecture. Given a scenario where BHappy needs dynamic tool approval (allow Bash for git but block for rm, allow Write only in worktree), design the permission system. Surface the allowed_tools vs can_use_tool misconception, then teach the correct model.

Worked Example: Cost tracking pipeline. Add total_cost_usd extraction from ResultMessage to BHappy's WorkerExecutor. Build PostToolUse hooks that log every tool invocation with timing, token count, and cost estimate into Postgres. Design the worker_attempts cost columns.

Guided: Distributed tracing. Design trace_id propagation: session → worker_attempt → tool_use chain. Implement PostToolUse and SubagentStart/Stop hooks that write structured trace events to Postgres. Build a query that reconstructs the full execution trace for a feature.

Conventional: Live session monitoring. Use ClaudeSDKClient with include_partial_messages for streaming progress to BHappy's dashboard via SSE. Track per-turn token usage and cost in real-time. Build cost anomaly detection (alert when session cost exceeds 3x baseline).

Mastery Gate: Run a BHappy worker with full instrumentation. Show: per-session cost in worker_attempts, structured tool-use log in Postgres, distributed trace reconstruction, live cost streaming to dashboard. Explain the can_use_tool vs allowed_tools architecture.

mastery_gate.criteria: Can instrument BHappy workers with cost tracking, structured logging, and distributed tracing. Can implement CanUseTool callbacks for dynamic permission decisions. Can build live session monitoring with streaming.

productive_failure_points.rationale: Calibration revealed incorrect mental model (session vs subagent scope). Productive failure surfaces this before instruction corrects it.
productive_failure_points.naive_theory: allowed_tools is session-scoped and can_use_tool is for subagents. Actually: allowed_tools is a static whitelist, can_use_tool is a dynamic runtime callback that inspects actual tool input.

task_classes.name: Agent Teams vs Subagents — Instrumented Comparison
task_classes.description: Instrument both TeamLauncher and WorkerExecutor with identical metrics. Build the A/B comparison framework with hard metrics to decide when to use Agent Teams vs sequential subagents. Use AGE for execution graph analysis.

tasks.description: Worked Example: Instrumentation parity. Add identical metric capture to both TeamLauncher (Agent Teams) and WorkerExecutor (sequential subagents): wall-clock time, total tokens, total cost, turns, tool uses, context utilization %, rework cycles, quality gate pass/fail. Design the comparison_runs Postgres table.

Guided: TaskNotification deep dive. Capture TaskStartedMessage, TaskProgressMessage, TaskNotificationMessage from Agent Teams runs. Build the timeline reconstruction: which agents ran when, how long, what they produced. Compare with sequential WorkerExecutor execution profile.

Guided: AGE execution graph. Model task dependency chains as AGE graphs: agents as vertices, dependencies/handoffs as edges, with properties for timing/cost/quality. Build queries: critical path analysis, parallelism efficiency, bottleneck identification. Compare Team vs Sequential graph structures.

Conventional: A/B decision framework. Run identical feature batches through both orchestration modes. Aggregate metrics. Build the decision matrix: feature size (XS→XL) × complexity × dependency depth → recommended mode. Add cost-aware model routing: when does Haiku-for-simple + Opus-for-complex beat uniform Opus?

Mastery Gate: Present the comparison results. Show: side-by-side metrics for Teams vs Sequential on real BHappy features, AGE graph visualizations of execution patterns, decision matrix with confidence intervals. Explain when each mode wins and why, backed by data.

mastery_gate.criteria: Can instrument both orchestration modes with identical metrics, reconstruct execution timelines from task messages, model execution as AGE graphs, and present a data-driven decision framework for Teams vs Subagents.

task_classes.name: Cross-Project Intelligence & Eval Framework
task_classes.description: Build pgvector semantic search over conversations, AGE graph relationships across projects, and the eval framework for measuring agent/skill quality over time. Lifetime replay and introspection.

tasks.description: Worked Example: pgvector embeddings for conversations. Design the embedding pipeline: extract meaningful chunks from session transcripts (decisions, tool outputs, reasoning), generate embeddings, store in pgvector. Build semantic search: 'what decisions were made about authentication across all projects?'

Guided: AGE cross-project graph. Model the full relationship graph: projects → sessions → agents → tool_uses → decisions → features. Build queries: 'show all sessions that modified auth.py across projects', 'trace the decision chain that led to the current database schema', 'find sessions where QA rejected work and developer fixed it'.

Guided: Eval framework foundation. Build scorecard-driven agent quality testing: define scorecards (agent-hiring-manager pattern), create trigger test sets (skill-creator pattern), run with/without-skill comparisons, assertion-based grading. Use structured_output for eval results.

Conventional: Benchmark and variance analysis. Run eval batches, aggregate pass rates with mean ± stddev, track quality trends over time. Build the lifetime replay: given any session_id, reconstruct the full execution with tools, decisions, and outcomes. Dashboard integration.

Mastery Gate: Full system demo. Semantic search across projects, AGE graph queries, eval framework running against a real BHappy skill, lifetime replay of a multi-session feature development. Present the architecture: how all TC1-TC4 components compose into the complete system.

mastery_gate.criteria: Can build semantic search over sessions with pgvector, model cross-project relationships in AGE, implement scorecard-driven eval framework with trigger testing and benchmarks, and demonstrate lifetime session replay. Can articulate the complete system architecture.

extended_roadmap.description: Beyond the 2.5-week sprint, continue building on the infrastructure with advanced capabilities.

phases.focus: Multi-team orchestration (dependent teams, cascading completions), adaptive model routing based on accumulated metrics, auto-scaling agent teams based on backlog depth
Use accumulated data for predictions: feature implementation time estimates, cost forecasting, quality risk scoring. ML models trained on the pgvector embeddings and AGE graph patterns.
Open-source the session storage backend, eval framework, and Teams vs Subagents comparison tooling. Contribute patterns back to the Claude Agent SDK ecosystem.

plateau_protocols.description: The backend abstraction layer design can feel like yak-shaving. The toggle between file and DB backends requires careful interface design that may feel tedious after the exciting AGE graph work.
plateau_protocols.breakthrough_strategy: Focus on the minimal interface: list_sessions() and get_session_messages() with identical signatures. Don't over-abstract — start with these two functions and extend later.

plateau_protocols.description: Agent Teams instrumentation can be frustrating because the Teams feature is experimental and completion detection is already complex (ADR-046). Adding metrics on top may feel like fighting the infrastructure.
plateau_protocols.breakthrough_strategy: Lean on what exists. BHappy already has ADR-046 completion detection with telemetry. The task is extending it with additional metrics, not rebuilding it. Keep the existing completion_metadata JSONB pattern.

motivation_architecture.identity_frame: You're becoming the architect who bridges Claude's agent infrastructure with production database systems — someone who doesn't just use the SDK but builds the observability and intelligence layer that makes autonomous AI development teams accountable and introspectable.
process_goals: Build or extend one working component of the session storage / observability system each session
Write at least one test for every new capability
Run at least one query against real BHappy session data per session
Document one architectural decision or tradeoff per day
Review the SDK changelog once per week and evaluate impact on the storage layer
